target: AG1’s claim that AI mainly improves convenience, health, learning, accessibility, and workplace safety, making it good for society overall.
objection: AI’s broader social impact is harmful: it displaces workers and shifts power toward big tech and capital owners, squeezes small businesses, undermines critical thinking, reproduces racism and discrimination from biased training data, and creates serious privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is net harmful because of jobs, critical thinking, bias, and privacy risks.
objection: Those harms do not justify rejecting AI outright because AI often automates routine tasks rather than eliminating whole jobs, can be used as a tutor that supports learning, can be audited and improved for fairness, and can be built with privacy protections; the right response is governance and responsible deployment, not blanket opposition.

target: AG1’s proposal that reskilling, classroom norms, auditing, and privacy safeguards can make AI’s risks manageable.
objection: That mitigation strategy is unrealistic because incentives and implementation realities make safeguards unreliable: job displacement and concentration of value outpace reskilling, AI use encourages outsourcing of reasoning, fairness audits cannot guarantee ongoing unbiased behavior, and privacy protections cannot fully prevent inference and surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are built into the technology and that management cannot make it overall beneficial.
objection: AI can still be overall good if society imposes structural governance such as impact assessments, post-deployment monitoring, human-in-the-loop rules, fairness requirements, and privacy safeguards, while also capturing concrete benefits in healthcare, education, accessibility, and workplace safety.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can contain misinformation and manipulation risks.
objection: Generative AI makes it cheap to mass-produce persuasive false text, images, audio, and video, enabling targeted propaganda, scams, and fake evidence at a scale that overwhelms verification and worsens polarization; this manipulation risk is hard to fully contain with governance.

target: AG2’s claim that AI-driven misinformation makes AI societally harmful overall.
objection: AI can also defend the information environment by flagging fake content, helping fact-checkers, adding provenance labels or watermarks, and scaling verification and takedown; the existence of misinformation risk does not erase AI’s net benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can defend against misinformation through detection, provenance, and rapid takedown.
objection: Those defenses are asymmetric and unreliable: detection lags creation, provenance tools can be circumvented or removed, and when defenses fail the burden falls on ordinary people, so the ecosystem still tilts toward deception and cognitive overload.

target: AG2’s claim that verification burdens the public and defenses are brittle.
objection: Governance can shift responsibility to platforms and deployers through liability, throttling, scam detection, authenticated content workflows, and restrictions on high-risk uses, so ordinary people do not have to bear the full verification burden.

target: AG1’s claim that platform liability, provenance systems, and restrictions can solve misinformation harms.
objection: Those fixes still fail because liability is hard to enforce, provenance and verification systems often expand logging and surveillance, and recommendation/engagement systems continue to manipulate attention and decisions at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that misinformation and other risks make AI harmful overall.
objection: AI need not be all-or-nothing; society can use targeted, tiered deployment that applies stricter controls to high-risk domains while preserving low-risk, high-benefit uses such as accessibility tools, translation, education support, and safety monitoring.

target: AG1’s tiered-deployment solution.
objection: Separating low-risk and high-risk AI use is fragile because tools can be repurposed quickly, low-risk uses still create data collection and platform dependence, and harms spill into everyday systems like recommendations, credit, hiring, and content visibility, disproportionately affecting racial minorities.

target: AG2’s claim that tiered deployment cannot address structural harms and spillover.
objection: Privacy-preserving design, interoperability and competition rules, and capability restrictions or licensing can reduce surveillance, lock-in, and mission creep while still allowing beneficial uses, so AI can remain net positive.

target: AG1’s privacy-preserving design, interoperability, and licensing proposal.
objection: Those remedies depend on costly technical choices and strong enforcement that providers will avoid or game; privacy-preserving methods are often less attractive, interoperability does not stop effective lock-in, and capability restrictions are porous because models diffuse faster than controls.

target: AG2’s claim that imperfect governance means AI is still net harmful.
objection: Even under imperfect governance, AI can still be overall good because high-value applications—especially in health—deliver concrete, time-sensitive benefits that do not require blanket surveillance or perfect control, and society can prioritize lower-misuse deployments.

target: AG1’s “benefits arrive faster than harms” argument.
objection: That time-horizon framing ignores that AI harms also occur immediately in high-stakes domains like medicine and education, and that societal welfare depends on who bears the costs: benefits often accrue to companies and adopters while harms are externalized to workers, marginalized groups, and the public.

target: AG2’s claim that benefits being distributed unevenly means AI cannot be socially good.
objection: AI can be used to reduce the very harms identified—decision-support in health, verification-support in education, and auditing for equity—so governance can convert major failure modes into targets for monitoring and improvement.

target: AG1’s claim that decision-support, verification-support, and fairness auditing can solve AI harms.
objection: Those mitigations depend on centralized data collection and continuous oversight, which intensify privacy risks and still fail to fully eliminate discrimination or overreliance; the needed monitoring and evidence pipelines are incomplete and privacy-invasive.

target: AG2’s claim that continuous oversight necessarily creates a privacy tradeoff and that AI should be rejected.
objection: Oversight itself can be made privacy-preserving through federated evaluation, differentially private metrics, and secure computation, and rejecting AI wholesale would deny marginalized groups and people with disabilities real accessibility and independence benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving oversight and assistive benefits make AI good overall.
objection: AI creates an accountability gap because people affected by automated decisions often cannot understand or challenge them; black-box systems in hiring, lending, benefits, policing, and education can deny due process and leave discrimination unaddressed.

target: AG2’s due-process objection about opaque automated decisions.
objection: Due process can be preserved by requiring contestability, practical appeals, qualified human review, standardized reason codes, and audit trails, which can make AI decisions more transparent and correctable.

target: AG1’s procedural due-process safeguards.
objection: Those procedural fixes often fail because human reviewers rubber-stamp AI outputs under time pressure and reason codes are superficial post-hoc summaries, so appeals become formalities while real decision power remains with opaque systems.

target: AG2’s claim that procedural fixes are insufficient because people still cannot challenge AI decisions.
objection: Real due process can be strengthened by requiring access to decision evidence through reason codes, human review, and logs, so appeals are not merely symbolic and AI can still be deployed without harming rights.

target: AG1’s claim that appeals and human review can preserve due process.
objection: Due process cannot work when AI systems change over time or produce nondeterministic outputs, because the decision being challenged is not stable or reproducible; that makes appeals symbolic and leaves the accountability gap intact.

target: AG2’s claim that model updates and non-reproducible outputs make AI decisions impossible to contest.
objection: Decision provenance measures such as model/version pinning, immutable logging, and reproducibility constraints can preserve stability and evidence for appeals even when models are updated, so the due-process gap is not inevitable.
